title: Meta open sources code to let you make Muse AI gadgets
content:
Meta now lets you make your own Muse gadgets that feature the company’s new AI agent with code that the company open sourced. The company suggests projects like loading Muse on a color E Ink display to show reminders, adding it to an HDMI stick so you can display Muse on a big screen, or putting Muse on a small touchscreen device to make what looks kind of like a DIY Muse Charm.
Meta open sources code to let you make Muse AI gadgets
Meta now lets you connect Muse to your own hardware to put on your displays or a Raspberry Pi.
“Muse gadgets are open source devices you build yourself,” Meta says. “Program an off-the-shelf ESP32 board or set up a Raspberry Pi with our SDKs, then connect Muse to your displays, buttons, sensors, actuators, and whatever else you’ve got lying on your workbench.” However, Meta cautions that you should “Proceed at your own risk!”
The company is also giving away a Muse Home Link gadget that it created. With the Muse Home Link, you use community-built skills to have the AI agent “turn on a light, control your TV, send a document to a printer, and more, depending on your setup,” Meta says. It manufactured 5,000 of the gadgets, according to Meta Superintelligence Labs’ Nat Friedman, and you can claim a waitlist spot for the Muse Home Link now ahead of shipping sometime this month.

report.summary: Meta open-sourced code and SDKs for DIY Muse AI gadgets, letting developers build AI devices on ESP32 or Raspberry Pi and claim a Muse Home Link hub.
report.background: Meta is trying to push its Muse AI agent beyond screens and into ambient, do-it-yourself hardware. The company has opened its SDK and code so makers can connect Muse to ESP32 boards, Raspberry Pis, displays, buttons, sensors, and actuators. This follows a broader trend of AI assistants becoming device-native, but unlike closed AI gadgets, Meta is betting on hobbyist ecosystems and community-built skills. Meta Superintelligence Labs, with Nat Friedman involved, is also shipping a reference device, Muse Home Link, with 5,000 units and a waitlist. The move taps the large ESP32 and Raspberry Pi maker market and positions Meta's agent as a layer for smart-home control and ambient computing, while cautioning users to 'proceed at your own risk.'
key_points: Meta released open-source code and SDKs for Muse gadgets, so anyone can build AI devices using off-the-shelf ESP32 boards or Raspberry Pi. Makers can connect Muse to displays, buttons, sensors, and actuators. Meta suggests projects like color E Ink reminder screens, HDMI sticks for big-screen Muse, and small touchscreen DIY Muse Charms, but warns users to proceed at their own risk.

The Muse Home Link is a ready-made reference gadget Meta is giving away. It uses community-built skills so the AI agent can turn on lights, control a TV, send documents to a printer, and more depending on your setup. Meta manufactured 5,000 units, and a waitlist is open ahead of shipping sometime this month.

The project is tied to Meta Superintelligence Labs, with Nat Friedman cited as saying 5,000 Muse Home Link units were made. This signals Meta's interest in open hardware and community skills rather than a fully closed AI gadget, potentially letting developers shape how the Muse agent works in physical spaces.

Meta's approach contrasts with recent standalone AI gadgets that struggled commercially. By targeting ESP32 and Raspberry Pi, Meta meets makers where they already are and lowers the cost of experimenting with AI-powered devices. However, support, security, and reliability remain open questions for early adopters.
report.impact: For the AI industry, Meta's move could accelerate a shift toward ambient, open, and DIY AI hardware, challenging closed AI gadget makers and making the agent layer more commoditized. Developers gain low-cost ways to prototype Muse-powered devices, but must handle privacy, security, and reliability without much hand-holding. Regular users may eventually get cheaper, personalized AI gadgets and smart-home control, though early versions will feel hackerish and limited. The 5,000-unit Home Link launch is small, so broad consumer impact depends on community momentum and whether Meta keeps supporting the SDK.
report.tools: To follow up, watch Meta's Muse SDK and the Muse Home Link waitlist, plus maker platforms like ESP32, Raspberry Pi, and Arduino. Smart-home stacks such as Home Assistant and ESPHome could bridge Muse skills to lights, TVs, and printers, while GitHub may host community-built skills. Suggested form factors include color E Ink displays, HDMI sticks, and small touchscreens.
